core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Part of optical-to-sonar transfer failure is the shading-direction prior: pretrained features interpret highlight-shadow patterns as 3D shading with light from above, so performance is sensitive to how the range axis is presented, and canonicalizing range axis orientation (or augmenting range-axis flips only during sonar fine-tuning) measurably changes accuracy in a way absent for scratch-trained models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fine-tuned ImageNet backbones will lose at least 2x more accuracy under test-time range-axis flips than under cross-track flips, while scratch-trained sonar models lose approximately equal amounts under both; kill the idea if the asymmetry ratio for pretrained models is below 1.3x or matches the scratch models.
why_important: Identifies which part of the optical prior is toxic for acoustic imagery, informing whether the field should canonicalize sonar geometry at input rather than hoping fine-tuning unlearns shading priors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Light-from-above priors are documented in human and machine vision; testing their interaction with sonar's sensor-fixed insonification direction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune an ImageNet ResNet and train a scratch twin on public sonar classification data with fixed range-axis convention, then measure the accuracy drop matrix under range-axis versus cross-track test-time flips for both models.
main_risk: Small public sonar datasets make scratch baselines weak, potentially conflating capacity effects with prior effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] ImageNet pretraining is assumed net-positive for sonar with any residual gap attributed to texture statistics, not directional shading priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may fully overwrite low-level shading priors even on small sonar sets, leaving no measurable asymmetry.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the Forward-Looking Sonar Marine Debris dataset (FLSMDD) with ResNet-18 (ImageNet weights vs scratch); the full flip matrix takes about 6 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$12).

one_line_idea: Sonar speckle is multiplicative with Rayleigh-family statistics, so augmentation and consistency training built on multiplicative noise should beat additive-Gaussian recipes imported from optical vision.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Coherent acoustic imaging produces speckle whose standard deviation scales with mean intensity (multiplicative), while default vision augmentation stacks inject additive Gaussian noise tuned for camera sensors.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Matching the augmentation noise family to the sensor's physics matters on small sonar datasets: multiplicative speckle-consistent augmentation (gamma-distributed intensity scaling with realistic correlation length) will yield better robustness and accuracy than additive Gaussian augmentation at any strength, because the invariances it teaches align with test-time variation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping augmentation strength for both families, the best multiplicative recipe will beat the best additive recipe by at least 3 accuracy points on cross-device sonar classification; kill the idea if the best-vs-best gap is under 1 point, which would say the noise family is a matter of indifference.
why_important: Sonar datasets are tiny and expensive; augmentation is the main lever, and the field currently imports optical recipes wholesale without checking the noise physics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Speckle models are standard in sonar/radar signal processing, but a best-vs-best augmentation family comparison with pre-registered margins on public sonar data appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid-sweep additive and multiplicative augmentation strengths on a public sonar classification task, select each family's best on validation, and compare on a held-out device or site split.
main_risk: If test-time variation is dominated by geometry (aspect, range) rather than speckle realization, both noise families will tie at a low ceiling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners assume noise-family details wash out after training and use default augmentation stacks from optical libraries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Log-transforming sonar intensities (common in preprocessing) converts multiplicative noise to approximately additive, potentially neutralizing the predicted difference.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: FLSMDD with ResNet-18; the two-family augmentation sweep is about 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$25).

one_line_idea: Sonar target signatures are so aspect-dependent that single-view recognition has a hard ceiling, and accuracy versus number of fused aspect views should follow a saturating information-accrual curve whose shape identifies the viewing-angle information content.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The acoustic return of an object changes drastically with insonification aspect (a cylinder end-on versus broadside looks like different objects); AUV surveys naturally acquire multiple aspects across passes, yet most ATR pipelines classify single snapshots.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Multi-aspect fusion yields accuracy gains that saturate only after several well-separated aspects, and the gain from a new view is predicted by its angular separation from already-seen views (large separation, large gain), reflecting genuinely complementary scattering information rather than mere ensemble averaging.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Fusing 3 views separated by at least 45 degrees will beat 3 views within 10 degrees by at least 5 accuracy points, and both will beat single-view; kill the idea if angular separation confers under 2 points over tightly clustered views, which would mean gains are just test-time augmentation.
why_important: This changes survey planning: if separation drives recognition, AUV paths should be optimized for aspect diversity, a free operational win with no new sensors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-view ATR exists, but the angular-separation-conditioned gain law that distinguishes physical complementarity from ensembling appears untested on public data.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Group multi-view detections of the same physical objects in a public sonar dataset by relative aspect, train a fusion classifier, and evaluate accuracy as a function of view count and angular spread.
main_risk: Public sonar data with repeated multi-aspect passes over identified objects is scarce; simulation with an acoustic scattering model may be needed to complete the aspect grid.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-view fusion is assumed helpful in a generic more-data sense, without the physics-grounded separation dependence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For simple proud targets, one broadside view may already carry nearly all discriminative information, flattening the curve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: FLSMDD (contains multiple captures of objects) plus simulated aspect sweeps from a point-scatterer model; ResNet-18 fusion experiments take about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20).

one_line_idea: Multipath ghosts in confined-water sonar occur at geometrically predictable offsets (surface/wall mirror images), so a geometry-conditioned deghosting filter can remove them and cut false positives without suppressing true nearby targets.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] In harbors, tanks, and near hulls, acoustic energy reflects off the surface and structures, producing ghost returns of real objects displaced along predictable mirror paths; detectors fire on ghosts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Given sensor pose and a coarse environment model (water depth, wall positions), ghost locations are computable as mirror-source images, so a filter that suppresses detections lying within the predicted ghost locus of a stronger detection will remove most multipath false positives while a naive non-max suppression over distance cannot.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Geometry-conditioned deghosting will remove at least 50% of multipath-attributed false positives at under 3% true-positive loss, and will beat distance-based NMS by at least 20 points of ghost-removal rate at matched true-positive loss; kill the idea if ghost positions fail to match mirror-geometry predictions within 2x range resolution for at least 60% of ghosts.
why_important: Confined-water inspection (hulls, harbors, aquaculture) is a major sonar use case where multipath is the dominant false-alarm source; a physics filter is auditable in ways a retrained black box is not.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multipath is modeled extensively in acoustics, but coupling mirror-source prediction to modern learned detectors as a post-hoc filter with pre-registered removal/loss budgets appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On tank-collected public sonar imagery, annotate ghost pairs, verify their geometric consistency with mirror-source predictions, then evaluate the filter against distance-based NMS on detector outputs.
main_risk: Ghost identification for evaluation requires care; mislabeled ghosts (real nearby objects) would understate true-positive loss.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multipath false alarms are treated as noise for the classifier to learn away, not as deterministic geometry to be computed and subtracted.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In cluttered environments the mirror model may be too coarse (multiple bounce paths), making predicted loci cover too much area and suppress real targets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: FLSMDD (collected in a water tank where surface/wall multipath is present) with a YOLOv8 detector; geometry filtering experiments run in about 5 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$10).

one_line_idea: Time-varying gain compensation residue leaves range-correlated intensity gradients in sonar images that models exploit as a positional prior, and randomizing gain profiles in training removes a measurable cross-platform transfer penalty.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sonar systems apply time-varying gain (TVG) to compensate spreading and absorption losses; compensation is never exact, leaving each platform with a characteristic residual intensity-vs-range profile baked into its imagery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on one platform partially key on its TVG residue, learning that target-like intensities at certain ranges are more or less credible; this manifests as range-dependent performance structure that tracks the training platform's gain profile and transfers poorly, and per-image gain-profile randomization (resampling the range-intensity curve within physical bounds) flattens it.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Detection recall binned by range will correlate with the training platform's residual gain profile (|r| >= 0.5), cross-platform transfer will show a reshuffled range profile, and gain randomization will cut the cross-platform mAP gap by at least 25%; kill the idea if the range-recall correlation is |r| < 0.2 or randomization recovers under 8% of the gap.
why_important: Cross-platform reuse of sonar models is blocked by opaque calibration differences; identifying TVG residue as a nameable culprit converts an intractable domain gap into a one-line augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Radiometric shortcuts are studied in optical remote sensing; the sonar TVG version with a randomization intervention appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate residual range-intensity profiles from background statistics on two public sonar datasets from different devices, train with and without gain randomization, and compare range-binned recall structure and transfer gaps.
main_risk: Range also correlates with true physical resolution and grazing angle, so profile-matched analysis must separate gain residue from genuine physics.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-device sonar failure is blamed on frequency and resolution differences; calibration residue is rarely named as a learnable shortcut.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern sonar processing chains may normalize backgrounds well enough that residual profiles are too small to be learned.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: FLSMDD plus the SeabedObjects-KLSG dataset (different devices) with YOLOv8; profile estimation and the randomization ablation take about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20).

one_line_idea: Cross-frequency sonar transfer is mostly a point-spread-function mismatch: matching resolution via physically derived PSF resampling recovers the bulk of the accuracy lost when models move between sonar frequencies.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Acoustic frequency sets an inherent resolution-range tradeoff; fleets operate sonars at different frequencies, and models trained at one frequency degrade at another, forcing per-device retraining.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant component of cross-frequency degradation is deterministic resolution mismatch rather than novel scattering physics, so resampling plus PSF-matched blurring of the higher-resolution data to emulate the lower-frequency system will recover most of the transfer gap, with the unrecovered remainder quantifying true frequency-specific scattering effects.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] PSF-matched emulation will close at least 60% of the cross-frequency classification gap; kill the idea if it closes under 25%, which would establish that frequency-dependent scattering (not resolution) dominates and PSF harmonization is a dead end.
why_important: Tells the field whether cross-device sonar portability is a signal-processing problem (solvable today with metadata) or a physics problem (requiring frequency-diverse training data).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution harmonization is routine in optical remote sensing; a decomposition of the sonar cross-frequency gap into resolution versus scattering components appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take two public sonar datasets at different frequencies with overlapping object categories, train at one frequency, evaluate at the other raw versus PSF-matched, and attribute the gap components.
main_risk: Overlapping category sets across public sonar datasets are limited, so the class intersection may be small and noisy.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cross-frequency failure is treated as an opaque domain gap requiring new labels rather than a partially deterministic transform.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Target strength and clutter statistics genuinely change with frequency (Rayleigh-to-geometric scattering transitions), possibly dominating the resolution effect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: SeabedObjects-KLSG and FLSMDD (different acoustic frequencies) with ResNet-18; PSF-matching experiments take about 8 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$15).

one_line_idea: Sonar detection difficulty is governed by the ratio of seabed ripple wavelength to target size, peaking near ratio one, giving a predictive environmental-difficulty law rather than a vague 'cluttered seabed' excuse.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection performance on sand-ripple seabeds is anecdotally poor, but 'clutter' is reported qualitatively; sand ripples have measurable wavelength and orientation from the imagery itself.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] False negatives and false alarms both peak when ripple wavelength is within roughly a factor of two of target extent, because ripple crests then mimic target highlight-shadow signatures at matched scale; difficulty falls off predictably on both sides of the ratio.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Binning detections by measured ripple-wavelength-to-target-size ratio will show a unimodal error peak within [0.5, 2] with error at the peak at least twice that at ratio 5 or 0.2; kill the idea if the error-vs-ratio curve is flat (max/min < 1.3) or monotone in overall ripple energy instead.
why_important: A quantitative environment-difficulty law lets surveyors predict per-area detection reliability from the imagery alone and plan re-survey or sensor changes where the ratio is unfavorable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ripple clutter is acknowledged in mine-hunting literature, but a scale-ratio law tied to modern learned detectors appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate ripple wavelength via 2D spectral analysis of background patches on public side-scan data, compute the ratio for each labeled target, and plot detector error rates against the ratio with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Public data may undersample the critical ratio range; simulated ripple fields with implanted targets may be needed to fill the curve.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Seabed type is treated as a categorical difficulty factor (sand/mud/rock) rather than a continuous scale-interaction with the target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned detectors may key on shadow continuity rather than scale-matched texture, making orientation (ripple direction versus range axis) the real driver instead of wavelength ratio.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: SeabedObjects-KLSG with a trained YOLOv8 detector; spectral binning and error analysis run in about 4 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$8).

one_line_idea: Synthetic aperture sonar micronavigation errors leave a characteristic azimuthal smearing signature from which the platform motion error is regressable, enabling learned autofocus that corrects imagery without inertial ground truth.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic aperture sonar coherently integrates pings along a track; unmeasured platform motion of a fraction of a wavelength defocuses the image with structured azimuth smearing, and classical autofocus is iterative and fragile in low-contrast scenes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mapping from defocused image patches to the low-order motion-error coefficients that produced them is learnable, because each motion mode (sway sinusoid, yaw ramp) imprints a distinct, physically determined blur signature; a regressor trained on physically simulated defocus generalizes to unseen scenes and enables one-shot refocusing.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The learned regressor will recover injected motion-error coefficients with R^2 >= 0.7 on held-out scenes and improve image sharpness (gradient energy) to within 20% of oracle refocusing; kill the idea if R^2 < 0.3 or if refocusing gains are less than half of what classical phase-gradient autofocus achieves on the same patches.
why_important: One-shot learned autofocus would cut SAS processing latency dramatically and rescue passes currently discarded, directly increasing area coverage rate for seabed mapping.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Learned autofocus exists in SAR literature; the sonar version with physically parameterized motion modes and a pre-registered comparison to phase-gradient autofocus appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate SAS defocus by applying parameterized along-track phase errors to well-focused public sonar imagery in the Fourier domain, train the coefficient regressor, and evaluate recovery and refocusing quality against classical autofocus.
main_risk: Real SAS raw data is mostly restricted; simulation-only validation limits the claim until a public raw dataset can be found, so real-data confirmation may require partnerships.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Autofocus is considered a solved signal-processing stage; learning is assumed to add nothing over model-based estimators.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scene-content diversity may swamp the blur signature, making coefficient regression scene-dependent and unreliable exactly where classical methods also fail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: SeabedObjects-KLSG imagery as focus substrate with a ResNet-18 regressor; simulation and training take about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20); real-SAS confirmation flagged as needing special data access.

one_line_idea: Predicting the acoustic shadow field from the highlight field is a physics-grounded self-supervised pretext for sonar encoders that beats generic contrastive pretraining in the low-label regime.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Labeled sonar data is scarce and expensive, while unlabeled survey imagery is abundant; generic self-supervision (contrastive/masking) imported from optical vision ignores sonar's paired highlight-shadow structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the shadow field is a geometric consequence of the ensonified scene (a projective function of elevation structure), training an encoder to predict masked shadow regions from highlight context forces it to internalize 3D seabed and object structure, yielding features that transfer to target classification better than modality-agnostic masking at equal unlabeled data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With 50 labels per class, shadow-prediction pretraining will beat masked-autoencoding pretraining by at least 4 accuracy points on sonar classification; kill the idea if the gap is under 1 point at every label budget from 10 to 200 per class.
why_important: A domain-native pretext converts every unlabeled sonar survey into structural supervision, directly attacking the field's central label-scarcity bottleneck.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Modality-specific pretexts exist elsewhere (e.g., colorization), but shadow-field prediction as sonar self-supervision appears unproposed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Segment shadows via intensity thresholding on unlabeled public side-scan mosaics, pretrain with shadow-region prediction versus standard masked autoencoding, then fine-tune both on label-budgeted classification splits.
main_risk: Threshold-derived shadow maps are noisy in low-grazing-angle regions, potentially teaching artifacts instead of geometry.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community ports optical self-supervision to sonar unchanged, assuming pretext choice is secondary to data volume.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Masked autoencoding may already implicitly learn highlight-shadow coupling, leaving no headroom for the explicit pretext.

one_line_idea: Defocus blur in single-plane brightfield microscopy carries recoverable axial (z) information, so a model can output a coarse depth map of subcellular structures from one 2D image, validated against real z-stacks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Microscopy analysis pipelines treat a single focal plane as a 2D image, discarding the fact that out-of-plane structures appear with defocus signatures (blur radius and contrast inversion) that are deterministic functions of axial offset under a known point-spread function.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The signed axial offset of cellular structures within roughly one depth-of-field unit is regressable from local defocus cues, because brightfield PSFs are asymmetric through focus; a network trained on z-stack supervision (offset planes as inputs, true offset as target) will produce usable coarse depth from single planes at test time.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-region axial offset regression will achieve mean absolute error below 0.5 depth-of-field units and correctly sign above/below focus for at least 75% of regions; kill the idea if signed accuracy is under 60% (near chance) or MAE exceeds 1 unit, which would mean single-plane defocus is not decodable.
why_important: Free 2.5D information from existing 2D assays would improve density estimates, colocalization judgments, and segmentation in thick samples without acquiring full z-stacks (10-50x less light and time, less phototoxic burden).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Depth-from-defocus is classical in photography and in-silico focusing exists, but a signed axial map of subcellular structures from single brightfield planes with pre-registered accuracy bounds appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From a public z-stack dataset, train on off-focus planes with known offsets, then evaluate signed offset prediction per region on held-out fields against the stack's true geometry.
main_risk: PSF asymmetry varies with optics and sample refractive index; a model trained on one instrument's stacks may not transfer, limiting the claim to per-instrument calibration.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Out-of-focus content is treated as degradation to be discarded or deconvolved, not as a depth signal to be decoded.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Brightfield through-focus behavior for transparent-phase objects may be too symmetric for reliable sign recovery without phase-contrast optics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: BBBC006 (Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection z-stacks of stained cells) with a ResNet-18 regressor; training and evaluation take about 6 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$12).

one_line_idea: Spectral bleed-through between fluorescence channels inflates in-silico labeling benchmarks: part of the reported ability to predict one stain from another is optics leakage, quantifiable by evaluating before and after linear unmixing.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fluorophore emission spectra overlap, so each acquired channel contains a linear mixture of other channels' signals (crosstalk); in-silico labeling models are trained to predict one channel from others and celebrated for learning biology.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable fraction of channel-prediction performance comes from physical crosstalk rather than learned biological correlation, so applying standard linear spectral unmixing to the inputs before evaluation will drop prediction fidelity by an amount that quantifies the optics-leak share, and this share varies strongly with fluorophore pairs' spectral overlap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For high-overlap fluorophore pairs, unmixing will reduce channel-prediction correlation by at least 0.1 (Pearson) while low-overlap pairs change by under 0.03, and the drop will rank-correlate with spectral overlap across pairs (rho >= 0.6); kill the idea if drops are uniformly under 0.03 or uncorrelated with overlap.
why_important: In-silico labeling is being adopted to replace physical stains; if part of its accuracy is crosstalk, deployments with different filter sets will silently underperform published numbers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crosstalk is a standard acquisition concern, but auditing learned cross-channel predictors for optics leakage with an overlap-ranked kill criterion appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public multichannel fluorescence dataset with known fluorophores, train channel-prediction models, estimate mixing matrices from single-stain controls or spectral references, and compare prediction fidelity on mixed versus unmixed inputs across fluorophore pairs.
main_risk: Unmixing itself introduces noise amplification, so a fidelity drop could partly reflect unmixing artifacts; noise-matched controls are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Channel-prediction success is read as evidence of biological structure learning, with acquisition optics assumed neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Well-designed public datasets may already use spectrally well-separated fluorophores, leaving little leakage to find.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the Human Protein Atlas multichannel images (or JUMP Cell Painting subset) with a U-Net predictor initialized from public Cellpose weights; the audit runs in about 12 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$25).

one_line_idea: Microscopy models are blind to physical scale because micrometers-per-pixel is stripped at training time; injecting physical pixel size as a conditioning token improves cross-magnification and cross-instrument generalization beyond scale augmentation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Cell and organelle sizes in micrometers are biologically diagnostic, but models receive raw pixels whose physical scale varies with objective and camera; standard practice is scale augmentation, which teaches scale invariance and thereby discards absolute size information.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There is a tension between scale invariance (helps nuisance robustness) and absolute-size sensitivity (carries biology); resolving it by conditioning on the known micrometers-per-pixel metadata (a physical token, not invariance) will beat both scale-augmented and non-augmented baselines on tasks where absolute size matters, especially transferring across magnifications.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On cross-magnification cell-type classification, metadata conditioning will beat scale augmentation by at least 3 accuracy points, with the advantage concentrated on size-discriminated classes (at least 2x the gain of shape-discriminated classes); kill the idea if conditioning gains under 1 point or shows no class-structure concentration.
why_important: Every microscope reports pixel size; using it is free and would make one model portable across objectives, a persistent pain point for core facilities.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Size-aware conditioning exists in spirit (diameter priors in cell segmenters); a controlled invariance-versus-conditioning comparison for classification transfer with class-structure analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble multi-magnification subsets from public datasets with pixel-size metadata, train the three variants, and evaluate cross-magnification transfer stratified by whether classes differ in size or in shape.
main_risk: Public multi-magnification data with consistent labels is limited; synthetic rescaling could substitute but weakens the instrument-transfer claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Scale augmentation is treated as strictly beneficial hygiene; the information it destroys is rarely discussed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may already infer physical scale from context (nucleus texture granularity), making explicit metadata redundant.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: Cell Tracking Challenge datasets (heterogeneous magnifications with metadata) with ResNet-18 and a FiLM-style conditioning layer; the comparison runs in about 10 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$20).

one_line_idea: Volume electron microscopy is physically anisotropic (section thickness >> lateral pixel size), and 3D models with anisotropy-matched receptive fields should beat isotropic-resampling pipelines on connectomic structures elongated along z.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Serial-section EM volumes have z resolution set by physical section thickness (tens of nanometers) versus much finer xy pixels; common pipelines resample to isotropic voxels or apply isotropic 3D kernels regardless.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Isotropic treatment mismatches the data's information geometry: interpolated z voxels contain no new information but consume capacity and blur boundaries, so architectures whose kernels and strides match the true anisotropy ratio will reconstruct thin z-elongated structures (axons crossing sections) more accurately than isotropic-resampled equivalents.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Anisotropy-matched models will reduce split-and-merge error rate (variation-of-information) by at least 10% relative on z-elongated structures while performing no worse laterally; kill the idea if the improvement is under 3% relative or if isotropic resampling wins on any anisotropy ratio above 3:1.
why_important: Connectomics throughput is bottlenecked by proofreading of split/merge errors that concentrate at section boundaries; matching architecture to acquisition physics is a zero-data-cost fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anisotropic kernels appear in some segmentation tools already, but a controlled law relating anisotropy ratio to the optimal architecture choice with a preregistered kill margin appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public EM benchmarks with different anisotropy ratios, train matched-capacity isotropic-resampled and anisotropy-native models and compare split/merge errors stratified by structure orientation.
main_risk: Capacity matching across kernel geometries is subtle; a sloppy match would confound architecture with parameter count.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Isotropic resampling is treated as harmless standardization inherited from medical imaging pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong learned priors may compensate for interpolation artifacts, making the architectural matching irrelevant at modern scale.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Public data and model: the MitoEM and CREMI EM benchmarks with public 3D U-Net baseline implementations; the comparison runs in about 24 GPU-hours on one consumer GPU (~$50).
